passages.happening:
Ahab has seventy sons in Samaria, brought up by the city's leading men. Jehu writes to the officials and guardians: choose the best of them, put him on his father's throne, and fight for your master's house (verses 1-3). They are terrified. ‘If two kings could not stand against him, how can we?’ (verse 4). They write back that they are his servants and will do whatever he says (verse 5).

Jehu's second letter demands the sons' deaths, and the men of Samaria carry it out and send proof to Jezreel (verses 6-8). The next morning Jehu tells the people, “You are innocent. It was I who conspired against my master and killed him. But who killed all these?” (verse 9). He says that ‘not a word the LORD has spoken against the house of Ahab will fail’ (verse 10). Then he kills everyone left of Ahab's house in Jezreel, with all his great men, his friends and his priests (verse 11).

On the road to Samaria he meets forty-two relatives of Ahaziah king of Judah, coming to greet the royal family. He has them taken and killed (verses 12-14). Then he meets Jehonadab son of Rechab, takes him into his chariot, and says, “Come with me and see my zeal for the LORD!” (verse 16). In Samaria he kills all who remain of Ahab's family, ‘according to the word that the LORD had spoken to Elijah’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
This chapter completes the destruction of Ahab's dynasty and of the Baal worship that Ahab and Jezebel had made the royal religion. It is the fulfillment of Elijah's word, and Jehu says so again and again.

In the ancient Near East the sons of a fallen dynasty were a standing threat to a usurper, and killing a previous king's family was a common, brutal practice. Jehu's letters shift the deed onto Samaria's leaders, and his speech plays on their guilt: he admits killing his master but asks who killed all these. The relatives of Ahaziah were princes of Judah, tied to Ahab's house by marriage, on a courtesy visit.

Jehonadab son of Rechab was the founder, or a leading ancestor, of the Rechabites, the clan that in Jeremiah's day still drank no wine and lived in tents out of loyalty to him. His presence beside Jehu signals the support of those who had resisted the Baal-worshiping court. The word for zeal, qin'ah, is used of God's own jealous love and of Phinehas, but also of human rivalry and envy. The chapter leaves open how much of Jehu's zeal was for God and how much for himself.
passages.later: Elijah had said to Ahab, ‘I will cut off from Ahab every male in Israel, both slave and free’ (1 Kings 21:21). In Jeremiah's day the Rechabites said, ‘our forefather Jonadab son of Rechab commanded us’ (Jeremiah 35:6), and they still kept his word.
passages.hard:
How should a reader take the killing of Ahab's sons and of Judah's princes?

The text tells it in a few verses and does not dwell on it, and these notes do the same. It presents the end of Ahab's house as the word of the LORD against innocent blood coming true. It also shows Jehu shifting the deed onto others, playing on their fear, and going beyond the word by killing the princes of Judah, who were not named in it. The narrator does not praise those parts, and a century later Hosea named the bloodshed as guilt on Jehu's house.

The sons of Ahab were in the care of guardians who handed them over to save themselves. The chapter does not call that right. Nothing here gives anyone a warrant to kill a rival's family, to purge opponents, or to call cruelty zeal for God.

A word for anyone who was not protected by a parent, or was handed over to harm by someone who should have kept them safe. This story does not call that right. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. If you are still in danger, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Jehu invited Jehonadab to come and see his zeal for the LORD. Ask how zeal for God can become mixed with a love of power or display. And ask whether you have ever shifted the blame for a wrong onto people who were afraid of you.

passages.happening:
Jehu gathers the people and says, “Ahab served Baal a little, but Jehu will serve him a lot” (verse 18). He summons all the prophets, servants and priests of Baal to a great sacrifice and says that whoever is missing will not live. ‘But Jehu was acting deceptively in order to destroy the servants of Baal’ (verse 19).

They come from all over Israel and fill the temple of Baal from end to end (verse 21). Jehu has vestments brought out for them, and with Jehonadab he checks that no servants of the LORD are among them (verses 22-23). He has eighty men posted outside. When the burnt offering is finished, he orders the guards in, and they kill the worshipers (verses 24-25). They bring out the sacred pillar of Baal and burn it, tear down the temple, and make it a latrine, ‘which it is to this day’ (verses 26-27). ‘Thus Jehu eradicated Baal from Israel’ (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Here the Elijah stories finally come to rest. The contest on Mount Carmel over whether the LORD or Baal is God ends with the destruction of Baal's temple in Samaria.

Jehu's trap uses the forms of Baal worship itself: a solemn assembly, special vestments and sacrifices in the temple. The sacred pillar, matsevah, was a standing stone representing the god's presence. Turning a temple into a latrine was a deliberate and lasting desecration. A similar act is known from archaeology at Lachish, where excavators of a gate shrine found a stone toilet they interpreted as deliberate defilement during a later reform in Judah.

The narrator names Jehu's method plainly. The word for his cunning, oqbah, is rare, and it is not praised. A reader is left to weigh whether the end justified the deception.
passages.later: In the contest on Carmel Elijah had asked the people, ‘If the LORD is God, follow Him. But if Baal is God, follow him’ (1 Kings 18:21). The law had said that Israel was to tear down the altars of the nations and smash their sacred pillars (Deuteronomy 12:3).
passages.hard:
How should a reader take Jehu's killing of the worshipers of Baal?

This is a violent scene, gained by a lie, and readers rightly feel its weight. The text tells it briefly, and these notes do not dwell on it. In its setting it is presented as the end of the royal cult of Baal that Ahab and Jezebel had built, a cult that had already killed the LORD's prophets. The law of Deuteronomy treated leading Israel to other gods as a capital crime against the covenant. And yet the narrator names Jehu's method as deception and does not praise it, and his heart, the chapter says, was not whole.

Christians broadly agree that such laws were for Israel as a nation under God's direct rule, at one moment in its story. The church was never given the sword. The New Testament meets false worship with teaching, prayer and discipline inside its own fellowship, and it leaves final judgment to God. When two disciples wanted to call down fire on a village that would not receive Jesus, ‘Jesus turned and rebuked them’ (Luke 9:55).

So it must be said plainly. This chapter gives no one today a warrant to harm, threaten or silence anyone over religion: not a person of another faith, not a person who has left the faith, not a family member.
passages.asks: Jehu won by deception, and the narrator does not hide it. Ask whether you have told yourself that a good end excused a dishonest means. And ask what in your own life you would be glad to see torn down, and what you would rather keep.

passages.happening:
Jehu ‘did not turn away from the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit’ (verse 29), the golden calves at Bethel and Dan. Even so, the LORD tells Jehu that because he has done well in carrying out what is right in God's sight, and has done to the house of Ahab all that was in God's heart, four generations of his sons will sit on the throne of Israel (verse 30). The next verse says, ‘Yet Jehu was not careful to follow the instruction of the LORD, the God of Israel, with all his heart’ (verse 31).

‘In those days the LORD began to reduce the size of Israel’ (verse 32). Hazael takes all the land east of the Jordan, Gilead and Bashan (verses 32-33). Jehu dies after twenty-eight years and is buried in Samaria, and his son Jehoahaz reigns (verses 35-36).
passages.hearers:
Jehu reigned about 841 to 814 BC. His dynasty lasted about a century, the longest in the northern kingdom, through Jehoahaz, Jehoash, Jeroboam II and Zechariah, four generations after him, as 15:12 notes. His coup cost Israel abroad. By breaking with Judah and with Phoenicia, Jezebel's homeland, and by paying tribute to Assyria, he left Israel alone. When Assyria withdrew from the west after about 838 BC, Hazael of Damascus was free to strike, and he took everything east of the Jordan.

Jehu removed Baal but kept the calves, the state religion that served his own interests. It is possible to oppose one idol with zeal while holding on to another. The word heart, levav, frames his story. He asks Jehonadab whether his heart is true; the LORD says he did all that was in God's heart concerning Ahab's house; and yet he did not walk in the LORD's law with all his heart.
passages.later: About a century later, the LORD told Hosea to name his son Jezreel, ‘for soon I will bring the bloodshed of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and I will put an end to the kingdom of Israel’ (Hosea 1:4).
passages.hard:
God praises Jehu, and Hosea later announces punishment on Jehu's house for the blood of Jezreel. How do these fit together?

Verse 30 has the LORD say that Jehu did well in doing to the house of Ahab all that was in God's heart, and it promises him four generations on the throne. About a century later the prophet Hosea named his son Jezreel and said that the LORD would bring the bloodshed of Jezreel on the house of Jehu. Readers have understood the tension in several ways.

One view holds that Jehu carried out God's judgment on Ahab's house but went far beyond it, killing Ahaziah of Judah and his relatives, the royal officials and priests, and doing it all with cruelty and for his own ends. Hosea condemns the excess and the motive, not the commission. A second view holds that Jehu's keeping of the calves showed his purge to be political rather than religious, so that the bloodshed God used for judgment became guilt on Jehu's own house. A third view, held by some critical scholars, sees two different prophetic judgments on Jehu preserved side by side.

All three agree that the chapter's own verdict is mixed, not simple praise, since verse 31 qualifies verse 30 at once. Being used by God to carry out judgment does not make anyone righteous. And nothing in Jehu's story gives anyone today a warrant for violence in God's name. The prophets who came after him did not hold him up as a pattern; they named his blood.
passages.asks: The narrator praises what Jehu did and then says his heart was not whole. Ask what the difference is between doing some right things and following God with your whole heart. And ask which idol in your life is easier to oppose because it does not serve your interests, and which one you have kept because it does.
